title: Governing Reserves: Managerial Discretion and Government Creditworthiness
authors: Sharon N. Kioko; Temirlan T. Moldogaziev
affiliations: Daniel J. Evans School of Public Policy and Governance University of Washington Seattle Washington USA; Paul H. O'Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs Indiana University Bloomington Indiana USA
abstract: ABSTRACT A government's ability to generate surpluses and build reserves reflects prudent financial management, with the accumulation of reserves signaling sound budgeting practices. Reserves are essential for sound fiscal governance during economic downturns, and managerial discretion over these resources is crucial to minimizing disruptions in service delivery. While the counter‐cyclical benefits of formal reserves are well documented, less attention has been paid to the discretion managers retain over reserves. Using credit ratings as a proxy for creditworthiness, we find that managerial discretion over accumulated resources enhances fiscal flexibility and strengthens creditworthiness; however, the presence of formal reserves alone does not improve credit ratings. Our study contributes to an emerging literature exploring whether better financial reporting can help us understand the critical balance between management flexibility and accountability mechanisms in public‐sector organizations.

title: Promises, Threats, and Norms: A Mixed Methods Study on Bureaucratic Support for Public Participation
authors: Jesse W. Campbell; Oscar Radyan Danar; Sanjay K. Pandey
affiliations: Department of Public Administration Incheon National University Incheon South Korea; Department of Public Administration, Faculty of Administrative Sciences Brawijaya University Malang Indonesia; Trachtenberg School of Public Policy and Public Administration George Washington University Washington DC USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Public participation can enhance policy quality and democratic legitimacy but may threaten bureaucratic control. We hypothesize that bureaucratic support for participation is higher when policies are less complex and participants are broadly representative. Using a mixed‐methods design involving Indonesian local public servants, we pursue complementarity by combining a 2 × 2 vignette‐based survey experiment with a Gioia analysis of qualitative reflections to explain the experimental results and further illuminate how bureaucrats evaluate participation. The experiment shows that participant representativeness significantly increases support, whereas policy complexity has no statistically significant effect. Integrating the experimental and qualitative data through joint displays reveals that bureaucrats rejecting participation frequently cite participant‐related risks, whereas supporters emphasize instrumental, procedural, and implementation benefits. Normative values, such as citizens' rights and democratic principles, are acknowledged regardless of bureaucrats' overall support. We conclude that bureaucratic support for public participation reflects how officials balance its promises, threats, and normative foundations.

title: Between the Lines: Decoding Signaling Differences in Public and Private Sector Job Advertisements
authors: Nico Gießmann; Nicolas Drathschmidt
affiliations: Institute of Human‐Centered Interactive Systems, University of Luebeck Lübeck Germany; Chair of Public and Nonprofit Management University of Potsdam Potsdam Germany
abstract: ABSTRACT To compete in the “war for talent,” public sector employers must demonstrate advantages over private employers. While public service motivation (PSM) predicts sector preference, scholars disagree on whether public employers (can) effectively signal PSM in job advertisements. Consequently, this article examines how public and private job advertisements differ in language. We collected 5000 advertisements from both sectors and performed natural language processing (NLP) and qualitative content analysis. Both sectors use specialized language that can narrow the applicant pool. PSM signals appear more often in the public sector, but affective motives are rarely communicated; instead, self‐sacrifice is framed as a legal obligation. Public sector advertisements adopt a rational tone instead of explaining purpose and societal value. Legally mandated, saturated signals may be perceived as low‐cost and ineffective. The findings explain the mixed results concerning PSM signaling and underscore the gap between theory and practice in PSM‐related recruitment efforts.

title: Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange
authors: Weixiao Huang; Carlos Morel Figueroa; Arjun Venat; Sarah E. Stanlick; Yunus D. Telliel; Alexander Teytelboym; Jennifer A. Pazour; Andrew C. Trapp
affiliations: Business School, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, New York 12180; Department of Computer Science, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Integrative and Global Studies, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Humanities & Arts, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Economics, University of Oxford, Oxford OX1 3UQ, United Kingdom; Business School, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; and Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, New York 12180
abstract: Unlocking Value Through Nonprofit Resource Sharing Nonprofit organizations often operate under tight budgets while idle equipment, unused space, and shareable skills and expertise are frequently underutilized, with existing resource exchanges in the nonprofit sector limited to bilateral barter or relatively homogeneous resources. In “Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange,” Huang et al. propose Sharing With a Purpose (SWAP), a resource-sharing system that enables nonprofits to exchange heterogeneous resources without monetary payments. SWAP combines an auction-based process, SWAPcredit valuation, and integer optimization to facilitate multilateral exchanges, allowing nonprofits to obtain needed resources by contributing resources of their own. The authors implement this market design through the SWAP Hub, a digital platform deployed with nonprofit communities in multiple regions. Through repeated exchange episodes, participating organizations have shared not only physical assets but also a wide range of skills, services, and expertise, including marketing, management, event planning, and organizational development. The study demonstrates how innovative market design can unlock latent value in community resources, alleviate resource constraints, and encourage new connections and collaboration among nonprofit organizations.

title: Optimality of Public Persuasion for Single-Good Allocation
authors: Chen Chen; Xuyuanda Qi
affiliations: New York University Shanghai, Shanghai 200124, China
abstract: When Sharing the Same Information Is Optimal Should a school advisor tailor recommendation letters to different employers or share the same information with everyone? Similar questions arise in start-up fundraising and biotech partnerships. In “Optimality of Public Persuasion for Single-Good Allocation,” Chen and Qi study how a sender can strategically disclose information when allocating an indivisible good to at most one self-interested receiver. The sender may send tailored private messages to individual receivers or publicly broadcast the same information to everyone. Surprisingly, the authors show that, when the sender has a known preference ordering over receivers, public persuasion is optimal even if receivers can subsequently communicate and share information. The optimal public mechanism can be derived from a simpler first-best allocation problem subject only to receivers’ participation constraints. The authors also develop a dual approach to characterize the structure of optimal mechanisms when the good’s characteristics are captured by a one-dimensional variable and all receivers’ utility functions are linear in this variable and reveal an intriguing decoupling structure.

title: Comment Letters, Connected Investors, and Corporate Bond Issuance
authors: Yi Ding; T. J. Wong; Ray Zhang; Tianyu Zhang
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Shenzhen 518172, China; University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90089; Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, British Columbia V5A 1S6, Canada
abstract: Using a proprietary data set that documents corporate bond issuances in China, we find that bond regulators’ comment letters (CLs) on issuers’ public disclosures generally target opaque firms and reduce bond issuance success. We also find, however, that connected investors—financial institutions with prior business relationships with the issuers—purchase a relatively larger share of bond issuances from CL recipients than from non-CL recipients, and this greater participation contributes to overpricing. Further analysis shows that connected investors support CL recipients because they possess superior private information and obtain private benefits from their connections. title: Enterprise Architecture Threat Modeling for Cybersecurity Risk Management
authors: Branko S. Bokan; Joost Santos
affiliations: The George Washington University Washington District of Columbia USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Organizations invest heavily in cybersecurity capabilities, yet the relationship between deployed defensive portfolios, practitioner judgments of coverage, and empirically observed adversary behavior remains difficult to assess. This study examines that relationship by integrating practitioner elicitation with threat‐informed cybersecurity architecture analysis. A model‐derived analytical baseline was constructed using the Cybersecurity Architecture Review (CAR) methodology aligned with MITRE ATT&CK version 17, quantifying protect, detect, and respond coverage for 12 commonly deployed cybersecurity capability categories. Survey data from 65 cybersecurity practitioners were used to characterize capability portfolios, perceived coverage, and factors influencing capability‐selection decisions. Results show uneven modeled coverage across the ATT&CK lifecycle and substantial functional overlap among capability categories. Across 910 respondent‐tactic observations, practitioner‐estimated coverage exceeded corresponding respondent‐specific modeled coverage by approximately 27 percentage points on average, although the magnitude and direction of perception‐model divergence varied by tactic. Most subgroup comparisons by professional role, responsibility, and experience did not identify statistically significant differences, while government respondents exhibited slightly higher mean divergence than nongovernment respondents in one pairwise comparison. Capability‐selection decisions reflected multiple organizational and external influences, with formal internal threat modeling reported less frequently than peer practices, regulatory or compliance requirements, independent research, and analyst or consultant reports. The findings demonstrate how threat‐informed architecture analysis can complement practitioner judgment by making modeled coverage, gaps, overlap, and divergence explicit within organizational cybersecurity risk governance.

title: Ambient Air Pollution Health Impacts in High‐Income Countries, Part II: A Case Study in the United Arab Emirates
authors: Tongchuan Wei; Nathan Ellermeier; Nick Kruskamp; Amal Mubarak Madhi; Latifa Juma Al Shamsi; Basema Ahmad Saddik; Jacqueline MacDonald Gibson
affiliations: Department of Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering North Carolina State University Raleigh North Carolina USA; Research Triangle Institute (RTI) International, Research Triangle Park North Carolina USA; Abu Dhabi Public Health Center Abu Dhabi UAE; Department of Public Health and Epidemiology, College of Medicine and Health Sciences Khalifa University Abu Dhabi UAE; School of Population Health, Faculty of Medicine University of New South Wales Sydney Australia
abstract: ABSTRACT Ambient air pollution poses major global public health risks, particularly in rapidly developing regions, including the Arabian Gulf. This study estimates the disease burden attributable to anthropogenic air pollution (particulate matter [PM] and ozone) in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, for 2019–2022 and compares findings to previous estimates for 2008. Burdens were calculated using updated air quality, population, and health incidence data for 2019–2022 along with concentration–response functions from recent epidemiologic evidence. Results show that Abu Dhabi's investments in air quality management have paid off in preventing air quality from deteriorating as much as would be expected given the doubling of the population between 2008 and 2022. However, epidemiologic evidence gathered during this period indicates that PM exposure has stronger negative effects on mortality risks than previously thought. As a result, estimated deaths attributable to anthropogenic ambient air pollution increased between 2008 and 2022, from 231 (90% uncertainty interval [UI]: 59–427) to 1249 (90% UI: 507–2169). Total hospital visits attributable to PM and ozone exposure also increased. These increases reflect combined effects of population growth, higher pollutant exposures, improved medical record‐keeping, and updated evidence on health risks. Urban centers, with higher pollutant concentrations and population densities, experience the highest risks, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to address air pollution hotspots. This work provides policymakers with up‐to‐date insights on the health impacts of ambient air pollution and underscores the importance of continued investments in air quality management in Abu Dhabi.

title: Triangulation as Methodology and Mindset: Developing Practice-Based Guidance for Organizational Research
authors: Sarah Wittman; Sébastien Point; Shiyu Yang
affiliations: Costello College of Business & College of Humanities and Social Sciences (Industrial-Organizational Psychology Department, by courtesy), George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA; EM Strasbourg Business School, Université de Strasbourg, HuManiS, Strasbourg, France; San Francisco State University
abstract: Aiming to inform organizational research practice, we scrutinize how scholars in management and business studies report triangulation: the systematic integration of multiple data sources, methodologies, measures, investigators, and/or theories, usually with the objective of enhancing the robustness, validity, richness, and/or complexity of research findings. We analyze 1,209 articles from the UTD24 journal list, using thematic analysis to assess scholars’ use and justification of triangulation as a term of art that spans disciplinary boundaries and qualitative, quantitative, mixed-methods, and nonempirical methodological approaches. Our findings elucidate triangulation types (method, data, investigator, theory, and measures triangulation); convergence (validity and corroboration) and divergence (richness and complexity) perspectives; and reporting practices at the manuscript level. From this analysis and our examination of exemplars, we abstract triangulation's dual nature: as a root methodology—a foundational tool that transcends methodological boundaries and is deployable across the research process—and a research mindset—an epistemological orientation that engages reflexivity and multiplicity to achieve rigor. Based on our findings, we provide recommendations for how to plan for, conduct, report, and evaluate triangulation and discuss our contributions to organizational research methods.

title: Correction
The Participation Gap: Reproducing Socioeconomic Inequality in Workplace Participation
authors: Jan Simon Danko
affiliations: University of Zurich, Switzerland
abstract: While workplace participation is widely endorsed as both a democratic ideal and a managerial imperative, access to it remains unequally distributed. Drawing on a Bourdieu-inspired organisational field perspective, this study examines how perceived inequalities in workplace participation are structured by class-based capital distributions and classed dispositions that align, or fail to align, with dominant organisational norms. Using original survey data from Switzerland, the article finds that individuals with higher socioeconomic standing report significantly greater access to workplace participation, even after accounting for their hierarchical position, educational attainment, and conventional sociodemographic factors. This relationship is mediated by classed dispositions differentially attuned to the rules of the game in the organisational field. The article thus challenges the normative assumption that participation inherently promotes equality, demonstrating that it can reproduce rather than redress social inequalities when underlying structural imbalances remain unaddressed.

title: Algorithmic management and the spatiotemporality of workarounds
authors: Lakshmi Narasimha Raju Vuddaraju; Sarah Hudson; Yi Liu
affiliations: Rennes School of Business, France
abstract: Existing literature on algorithmic management has explored how workers respond to algorithmic control using workarounds. However, the role of spatiotemporal factors in shaping these workarounds is largely overlooked. This study therefore examines how workers use spatiotemporal workarounds in response to algorithmic management. We integrate Lefebvre’s spatial triad and rhythmanalysis to analyse data from an online community of Amazon delivery drivers. Our findings show how delivery drivers proactively adapt to spatiotemporal constraints imposed by algorithms by modifying their routes, adjusting the pace and rhythm of their work and using workarounds to proactively influence future algorithmic decisions. Our study contributes to the growing literature on the spatiotemporality of algorithmic work, highlights the role of humans as proactive agents in shaping algorithmic decisions and exerting temporal sovereignty and reconceptualises workarounds as dynamic, evolving and future-oriented adaptations rather than immediate resistance tactics.

title: Affective order of time discipline: The emotional foundation of time pressure in the online gig economy
authors: See Pok Loa
affiliations: School of Management, University of Leicester, UK
abstract: This article examines how being pressed for time can be internalised as a compulsive and deeply entrenched experience through emotions in the Chinese online freelancing labour market. It advances EP Thompson’s concept of time discipline, while drawing on the literature of labour time, speed-up society and emotion. The analysis identifies three types of affective dispositions – anxiety, pride and contentment – that underpin the cultural notations and disciplinary power of time discipline. They are termed affective order of time discipline . This theorisation reasserts the centrality of the ‘inward notation’ of time and demonstrates how they are sustained through emotional mechanisms, thus explaining the internalisation depth and breadth of time discipline. These insights imply that the reproduction of time pressure on platforms is not just an artefact of technological infrastructures. Rather, to reclaim time, time-related feelings constitute key sites to be ‘undisciplined’.

title: Ownership and Confusion in Employee‐Owned Firms: An Exploration of the EOT Model
authors: Jonathan Preminger; Dimitrinka Stoyanova Russell
affiliations: Cardiff Business School Cardiff University Cardiff UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Based on interviews with employees in UK employee ownership trusts (EOTs), this article interrogates understandings of ‘ownership’ and explores confusion, tensions and frustrations in the lived experience of ownership stemming from employees' dual status as employees and owners. Employees assume that ownership brings various rights, but these often conflict with management understandings, the perspectives of other employees and the limited rights legally embedded in the EOT model. This emphasises the tensions between employee‐owners' legal status as beneficiaries and aspects of their ownership status that are dependent on norms and discourse. Relationships are crucial in developing shared understandings of ownership within the internal ‘community’ of employee‐owners. By showing how relationships shape such understandings and how ownership ‘works’ in practice, the study illuminates how conceptualisations of ownership impact the functioning of EOT firms.

title: Service Recovery in Chatbot‐mediated Environments: Trust Dynamics and Customer Loyalty Intentions
authors: Wilson Ozuem; Silvia Ranfagni; Michelle Willis
affiliations: University of Cumbria, Institute of Business, Industry and Leadership UK; University of Florence, Department of Economics and Business Sciences Italy; University of Roehampton, Faculty of Business and Law UK
abstract: Abstract Prior research has shown that customers’ perceptions of chatbots may be influenced by the situational context in which human–chatbot interactions take place. This research advances understanding of artificial intelligence (AI)‐enabled chatbot‐led service failure recovery (SFR) in the context of customer loyalty. Using a social constructivist philosophical perspective and an inductive approach, 52 in‐depth interviews were conducted to capture individuals’ perceptions of chatbot‐led interactions during a SFR process and how these perceptions impacted their trust in, and commitment to, brands. Utilizing commitment‐trust theory and trust transfer theory, we propose a framework that characterizes the relationships between a chatbot‐led SFR process and customer loyalty intentions. Based on the emergent data, customers’ evaluations of a service recovery journey led by chatbots can be grouped into four main outcomes: continued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand; continued trust in, and commitment to, brand; discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot; and discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand. Our findings extend current understanding of how consumers’ trust and commitment during chatbot‐led interactions during SFR evolve and highlight the dynamic relationship between consumers and the context of interactions. This study has theoretical and practical implications for developing and leveraging customers’ loyalty in AI‐enabled chatbot‐led SFR environments.

title: Value creation and capture in artificial intelligence‐enabled ecosystems
authors: Rahul Kapoor; Manav Raj
affiliations: The Wharton School University of Pennsylvania Philadelphia Pennsylvania USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.

title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
authors: Andy Wu; Ronald Wang
affiliations: Strategy Unit, Harvard Business School Harvard University Boston Massachusetts USA; Department of Management Science and Engineering Stanford University Stanford California USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

title: Trade, Human Capital, and Income Risk,
authors: Liuchun Deng; Pravin Krishna; Mine Z Senses; Jens Stegmaier
affiliations: Duke Kunshan University, China and Halle Institute for Economic Research ,; Johns Hopkins University ,; Institute for Employment Research ,
abstract: Abstract In this paper, we study the causal relationship between trade exposure and individual income risk, with emphasis on the role of human capital. We use a rich worker-level longitudinal dataset from Germany spanning the period 1976-2012, and find industry trade exposure to be causally related to income risk: Imports increase risk and exports decrease risk in an economically significant manner. Importantly, there is a complex interplay between human capital and the linkage between trade and risk: On average, individuals with higher levels of industry- or occupation-specific human capital experience lower risk. However, an increase in industry net imports increases risk more for workers with higher levels of industry tenure. Although net imports are also associated with declines in the mean income of these workers, the estimated effect on income levels is economically small. Our welfare framework, which jointly considers both mean income and income risk, shows that the welfare consequences of trade exposure are quantitatively dominated by the risk channel.

title: TESTING FOR ENDOGENEITY: A MOMENT-BASED BAYESIAN APPROACH
authors: Siddhartha Chib; Minchul Shin; Anna Simoni
affiliations: WUSTL; Philadelphia Fed; CNRS
abstract: A standard assumption in the Bayesian estimation of linear regression models is that the regressors are exogenous in the sense that they are uncorrelated with the model error term. In practice, however, this assumption can be invalid. In this article, using the exponentially tilted empirical likelihood (ETEL) framework, we develop a Bayes factor test for endogeneity that compares a base model that is correctly specified under exogeneity but misspecified under endogeneity against an extended model that is correctly specified in either case. We provide a comprehensive study of the log-marginal ETEL. We demonstrate that our testing procedure is consistent from a frequentist point of view: as the sample grows, it almost surely selects the base model if and only if the regressors are exogenous, and the extended model if and only if the regressors are endogenous. The methods are illustrated with simulated data and problems concerning the causal effect of automobile prices on automobile demand and the causal effect of potentially endogenous airplane ticket prices on passenger volume.

title: PROXIMAL ESTIMATION AND INFERENCE
authors: Alberto Quaini; Fabio Trojani
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam; University of Geneva, Swiss Finance Institute, and Collegio Carlo Alberto
abstract: Abstract We develop a convex-analytic framework for constructing and analyzing a broad class of penalized estimators. Our method defines penalized estimators by applying proximal operators to benchmark estimators, rather than by penalizing the benchmark criterion itself. We establish general finite-sample properties, derive unified asymptotic distribution results, and provide tractable conditions for oracle selection and oracle asymptotic efficiency. We then apply the framework to linear regression with irregular designs, including singular and nearly-singular cases. In this setting, where the coefficient vector need not be point identified, we motivate the Ridgeless estimand as the inferential target, construct a n $\sqrt {n}$ StartRoot n EndRoot -consistent modified Ridgeless benchmark estimator, and combine it with adaptive proximal penalization to obtain, to the best of our knowledge, the first penalized estimator achieving the oracle property under both regular and irregular designs.

title: Risk, Specialization, and Covered‐Interest Parity
authors: TOBIAS J. MOSKOWITZ; CHASE P. ROSS; SHARON Y. ROSS; KAUSHIK VASUDEVAN
abstract: ABSTRACT Prevailing theories of financial intermediation assume an integrated financial sector with frictionless risk‐sharing. However, we identify substantial risk‐sharing frictions linked to intermediary specialization using currency derivatives markets as a laboratory. Using confidential supervisory data covering $25 trillion in daily bank exposures, we document imperfect hedging in banks' FX‐swap intermediation: banks rarely hedge their synthetic dollar lending with maturity‐matched foreign safe assets. Intermediaries specialize in markets in which they have expertise in managing the associated exposures, giving rise to cross‐market variation in deviations from covered‐interest parity. Our results highlight the importance of intermediary specialization and its impact on risk premia.

title: Externalities of Responsible Investments
authors: MICHELE BISCEGLIA; ALESSIO PICCOLO; JAN SCHNEEMEIER
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a model to study the efficiency of socially responsible investing (SRI) as a mechanism to control firms' externalities. When SRI is not too popular, responsible investors favor strategies that lead to a concentration of SRI in a subset of firms in the economy. This concentration can mitigate coordination issues in adopting green technologies, but it can also crowd out the green investments of excluded firms and increase the price of green products. In equilibrium, responsible investors continue to favor concentration even as SRI becomes more popular, and concentrate the most when concentration is least desirable.

title: Determinants and Consequences of Auditors’ Consultations with the National Office
authors: Matthew G. Sherwood; Miguel Minutti-Meza; Aleksandra B. Zimmerman
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst; University of Miami; Florida State University
abstract: ABSTRACT Audit teams may consult with their firm’s national office to obtain specialized expertise, satisfy regulatory and quality control requirements, and demonstrate due professional care. We describe the consultation process based on PCAOB standards, firm methodologies, and auditor interviews. We explain different types of consultations and highlight differences in the determinants and usefulness of mandatory versus voluntary consultations. Using PCAOB inspection data, we show that formal consultations are largely predictable based on engagement characteristics and, on average, are not associated with audit quality. However, two subsets of formal consultations that focus on accounting issues and occur earlier in the engagement process are associated with greater regulatory compliance and higher audit quality. Hence, an increasing reliance on all types of consultations does not automatically translate into higher audit quality. Collectively, our findings deepen our understanding of auditors’ use of national office consultations and their implications for audit practice. Data Availability: Audit engagement data from the PCAOB are proprietary; other data are from public sources. JEL Classification: M4.

title: Unintended Regulatory Spillovers: The Impact of Bank Regulatory Oversight on Environmental Enforcement
authors: John Gallemore; Vincent Giese
affiliations: University of North Carolina; University of Mannheim
abstract: ABSTRACT We explore whether bank regulatory oversight affects the ability of environmental enforcement to reduce industrial emissions. A major objective of environmental enforcement is to reduce industrial emissions by encouraging firms to employ greener production processes and technologies. However, such changes often require external financing obtained from banks, and prior research shows that regulatory oversight of banks can affect bank lending. We find that, on average, the reduction in air pollution in response to county‐level environmental enforcement is attenuated in counties exposed to increased bank regulatory oversight, as measured by severe enforcement actions. Furthermore, we show that the negative impact of bank regulatory oversight on small business lending to affected counties is the likely mechanism behind this on‐average effect. However, when bank regulatory oversight targets banks with stronger capitalization, we find that the negative effect of bank regulatory oversight on environmental enforcement is mitigated. Collectively, our findings suggest that bank regulation has a nuanced effect on the extent to which environmental enforcement reduces emissions, indicating that one regulator's mission can impact the objectives of another.

title:
Would a Balanced
                    <scp>PCAOB</scp>
                    Inspection Approach Increase Auditors' Use of Innovative Audit Procedures?
authors: Yoon Ju Kang; M. David Piercey
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst Amherst Massachusetts USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research criticizes PCAOB inspection reports for focusing solely on audit deficiencies, arguing that this encourages auditors to pursue traditional procedures to demonstrate compliance with standards rather than procedures that maximize audit quality. We contribute to this debate by examining whether the PCAOB's approach discourages auditors from considering innovative audit procedures (that are potentially more effective), since they are, by definition, less standard. We compare the PCAOB's current inspection approach (which focuses on reporting audit deficiencies) to a balanced inspection approach that discloses examples of audit strengths as well as deficiencies discovered during inspections. We predict and find that when the risk of material misstatement (RMM) is moderate, a balanced inspection approach leads auditors to consider the potential effectiveness of innovative audit procedures to a greater extent, ultimately prioritizing more of them in audit plans. Our findings contribute to both research and practice by enhancing our understanding of ways to encourage audit innovation and ultimately improve overall audit quality.

title: Could That Happen to Me? Auditor Response When Colleagues Are Named in Lawsuits
authors: Brant E. Christensen; Nathan G. Lundstrom; Nathan J. Newton
affiliations: Brigham Young University Provo Utah USA; University of Kansas Lawrence Kansas USA; Florida State University Tallahassee Florida USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Litigation risk is an important source of motivation for auditors to conduct high‐quality audits, but theory suggests that certain lawsuits will have a more salient disciplining effect on auditor behavior. To this end, we identify lawsuits naming an individual partner as a co‐defendant along with the audit firm. We then examine how these lawsuits affect subsequent behavior of other auditors in the office of the sued partner. Relative to lawsuits naming only the firm, our results indicate that lawsuits naming individual partners as co‐defendants are significant office‐level events that motivate a meaningful response from non‐sued audit partners in the form of higher quality and fees on existing clients and more careful client portfolio management. These results have practical implications about how auditor litigation incentivizes individual auditors to fulfill their professional duties. For regulators and audit firms seeking to promote audit quality, these findings highlight the disciplining effect of auditors' concern for their personal reputation and litigation exposure. Furthermore, audit committees, clients, and investors may observe elevated audit quality, effort, and fees following partner‐level litigation in the local office.

title: Public Service Decline and Support for the Populist Right: Evidence from England’s National Health Service
authors: ZACHARY P. DICKSON; SARA B. HOBOLT; CATHERINE DE VRIES; SIMONE CREMASCHI
affiliations: London School of Economics and Political Science; IE University; University of Oxford
abstract: The rise of populist right parties is well studied, but relatively little attention has been given to how public service performance influences voter support. Given that public services are often the primary means through which citizens interact with the state, we argue that declining public services can create grievances that increase the appeal of populist right parties. Focusing on England’s National Health Service, we combine administrative data on local health facility closures with panel data on public preferences and voting intentions. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that closures reduce satisfaction with public services and increase support for populist right parties. These effects are moderated by migrant registrations at local health practices, highlighting the interaction between public service performance and immigration concerns in fueling populist right support. Our findings underscore the role of public service decline as a driver of support for populist parties, especially in areas undergoing demographic change.

title: Issue Information
Spatiality of preemptive coercion: How autocrats demolish informal settlements for political control
authors: Shiqi Ma
affiliations: Department of Politics and International Studies SOAS University of London London United Kingdom
abstract: Abstract Why do authorities demolish informal settlements in metropolises? The social sciences have a long tradition of addressing this issue through the lens of economic development or welfare provision. I instead propose a theory of political control. Autocrats adopt demolition as a preemptive and coercive tool to remove communities substantively and symbolically less legible to them, thereby ensuring societal compliance and restoring visual order. Empirically, I compile a unique dataset of 320 demolished and undemolished informal settlements in Beijing between 2017 and 2018, based on satellite imagery, digital street views, and fieldwork. The results indicate that the low legibility of informal settlements to authorities correlates with a greater likelihood of demolition. This paper contributes to the social science literature by connecting legibility politics with urban governance. It also introduces a spatial perspective and leverages novel data sources to deepen our understanding of preemptive coercion under authoritarianism.
